entries.title: Effort level
entries.summary: A setting (increasingly available in 2026) that controls how much reasoning the AI applies to your request. Low effort = fast, shallow, cheap. High effort = slow, thorough, expensive. You're trading speed for depth. Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Embedding
entries.summary: A list of numbers that represents the meaning of a piece of text — arranged so that similar meanings sit near each other Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Emergence
entries.summary: Capabilities that appear unexpectedly as models get larger — abilities no one programmed in Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Endpoint
entries.summary: A specific URL where you send requests to use a model via API — like an address for the model's "office" Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Evals
entries.summary: Custom evaluation tests a company builds for its specific use case — "does our model get THIS right?" Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Evaluation
entries.summary: The skill of judging whether AI output is actually good, not just fluent-sounding Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Evaluation rubric
entries.summary: A set of specific questions you check output against: Is it accurate? Is it complete? Is it relevant? Is it appropriate for the audience? Having defined criteria is faster and more reliable than "does it feel right?" Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Export controls
entries.summary: Government restrictions on selling advanced technology to specific countries — the US restricts AI chip sales to China Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Fabrication plant (fab)
entries.summary: The physical factory where chips are manufactured. Costs $10–20 billion to build Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Failure mode
entries.summary: A specific way the output could be wrong that you'd reject. Stating these upfront prevents the AI from going in a direction you'll discard. Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Few-shot examples
entries.summary: Showing the AI 2-3 concrete examples of the input-output pattern you want, instead of (or in addition to) describing what you want in words. Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Few-shot prompting
entries.summary: Including examples of what you want directly in your prompt — "here are 3 examples, now do the 4th" Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Fine-tuning
entries.summary: Additional training on a smaller, specific dataset — adjusting the model's weights for a particular domain or behaviour Read the full explanation .

entries.title: FLOPS
entries.summary: Floating-point operations per second — a measure of raw processing power Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Forward diffusion
entries.summary: The training process of adding noise to an image until it's pure static Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Foundry
entries.summary: A factory that manufactures chips designed by other companies. TSMC doesn't design chips — it builds them for NVIDIA, Apple, AMD, and others Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Generative AI
entries.summary: AI that creates new things (text, images, code, audio) rather than just sorting or recognising Read the full explanation .

entries.title: GPU (Graphics Processing Unit)
entries.summary: Originally designed for rendering graphics; turns out to be perfect for AI because it does thousands of simple calculations simultaneously Read the full explanation .
aliases: what does GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) mean

entries.title: Gradient descent
entries.summary: The method for adjusting weights in the right direction — like rolling downhill toward the lowest error Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Graph engineering
entries.summary: Wiring multiple agents/loops into an orchestrated system — nodes, edges, parallel branches, handoffs (July 2026) Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Grounding
entries.summary: When AI's response is based on actual source material (a document, a search result, your data) rather than generated from its training. Grounded answers are more trustworthy. Ungrounded answers may be hallucinated. Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Guardrails
entries.summary: Product checks or rules that may inspect an input, a proposed action or an output and then allow, refuse, limit, redact or escalate it. Their coverage varies, and they can miss or over-block. Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Hallucination
entries.summary: The model generating confident-sounding output that isn't true — a structural consequence of predicting probable tokens, not retrieving verified facts Read the full explanation . Put it into practice .

entries.title: Harness
entries.summary: The operating layer around the model — manages context assembly, tool access, memory, quality gates, and the control loop Read the full explanation . Put it into practice .

entries.title: HBM (High Bandwidth Memory)
entries.summary: Specialised memory stacked on top of GPUs — essential for AI, manufactured primarily in South Korea (Samsung, SK Hynix) Read the full explanation .
aliases: what does HBM (High Bandwidth Memory) mean

entries.title: Hedging
entries.summary: When the AI refuses to commit to an answer: "It depends," "There are many factors," "This is a complex issue." Sometimes appropriate. Usually a crutch. Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Human-in-the-loop
entries.summary: The system pauses before acting and asks a human for approval — a safety checkpoint Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Hyperscaler
entries.summary: A company that operates data centres at massive scale: Amazon (AWS), Microsoft (Azure), Google (GCP), Meta Read the full explanation .

entries.title: img2img (image-to-image)
entries.summary: Generating a new image using an existing image as the starting point instead of pure noise Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Inference
entries.summary: Using a trained model to generate output — applying the learned patterns to new input. The "job" after "school." Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Inpainting
entries.summary: Editing only a specific region of an image while leaving the rest untouched Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Input tokens
entries.summary: The tokens in what you send (your question, your document, the conversation history) Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Integration / MCP
entries.summary: A connection between the AI and another app or data source. Think of it like a USB-C port: one standardised plug that connects to many different things. When your AI is "connected" to your email, calendar, or files, it can read from and sometimes act on those systems. Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Jagged frontier
entries.summary: AI's capability boundary isn't a smooth line where hard tasks are on one side and easy tasks are on the other. It's ragged: AI is brilliant at some hard things and terrible at some easy things, in patterns you can't always predict in advance. Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Jailbreaking
entries.summary: Techniques that trick the model into bypassing its safety training — getting it to produce content it was trained to refuse Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Knowledge cutoff
entries.summary: The date at which training data was locked — the model doesn't know anything that happened after this point Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Labelling
entries.summary: Humans marking examples as "this" or "not this" so the machine can learn the difference Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Labelling / annotation
entries.summary: Humans marking examples with the right answer ("this is spam," "this is a cat," "this response is better than that one") so the system can learn what "correct" looks like Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Latency
entries.summary: How long you wait for a response — the time between pressing "send" and seeing the first word appear Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Liquid cooling
entries.summary: Using liquid (not air) to cool chips — increasingly necessary as AI chips generate more heat than air cooling can handle Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Lithography (EUV)
entries.summary: The process of etching chip patterns using extreme ultraviolet light. Only one company makes these machines: ASML (Netherlands) Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Loop engineering
entries.summary: Designing the execution cycle an agent runs in — triggers, stopping conditions, iteration limits, feedback mechanisms (June 2026) Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Loss function
entries.summary: The measurement of "how wrong was that guess?" — the score the system is trying to minimise Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Lost in the middle
entries.summary: A documented property of AI models: they pay the most attention to the beginning and end of what they can see, and less attention to everything in between. Read the full explanation .
aliases: what is Lost in the middle
what does Lost in the middle mean

entries.title: Machine learning
entries.summary: The broad category: a system that learned patterns from data (everything from Chapter 1) Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Machine learning engineer
entries.summary: Takes research and builds it into working systems that run at scale. The bridge between research and production. Read the full explanation .
aliases: what does Machine learning engineer mean

entries.title: Maintenance
entries.summary: The occasional work of keeping your system current: updating instructions that have gone stale, testing new tools on your actual tasks, and adjusting what you delegate as the frontier moves. Read the full explanation .

entries.title: MCP (Model Context Protocol)
entries.summary: An open standard (Anthropic, 2024) that standardises how agents discover and use tools — the "USB-C for AI tools" Read the full explanation .
aliases: what does MCP (Model Context Protocol) mean

entries.title: Memory
entries.summary: Facts the AI accumulates from your conversations and remembers across sessions. Some tools do this automatically; others need you to ask. Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Memory (in AI)
entries.summary: Not actual memory — information stored externally and re-injected into the context window each time. The model itself remembers nothing. Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Mixture of Experts (MoE)
entries.summary: A model architecture where only a small fraction of parameters activate for any given token — big capacity, lower compute Read the full explanation .
aliases: what does Mixture of Experts (MoE) mean

entries.title: MLOps engineer
entries.summary: Keeps ML systems running in production — deployment, monitoring, scaling, versioning. Read the full explanation .

entries.title: MMLU
entries.summary: A benchmark testing knowledge across 57 academic subjects (like a multi-subject exam) Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Model
entries.summary: The finished product of training — architecture + learned weights. The thing that takes input and produces output. Read the full explanation . Put it into practice .

entries.title: Model collapse
entries.summary: When AI trains on AI-generated data across multiple generations, progressively losing diversity and accuracy until the output becomes bland and narrow Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Multi-agent system
entries.summary: Multiple agents working together — collaborating, specialising, or handing tasks between each other Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Multimodal
entries.summary: A model that handles multiple types of input/output (text, images, audio, video) in one system Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Multimodal input
entries.summary: Giving the AI something other than text: images, screenshots, photos, audio, or video. Most major tools now handle all of these. Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Narrow AI / ANI
entries.summary: What we have today. AI that's excellent at specific tasks but can't generalise. A chess AI can't write poetry. A language model can't play chess at superhuman levels (without tools). Read the full explanation .
aliases: what does Narrow AI / ANI mean

entries.title: Native audio
entries.summary: Processing voice directly as audio tokens, without converting to text first Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Neural network
entries.summary: Layers of simple maths operations that transform input into output — each layer adjusts the signal slightly Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Node (e.g., 3nm, 5nm)
entries.summary: A measure of chip manufacturing precision. Smaller = more transistors = faster, more efficient. Leading edge in 2026: 3nm, with 2nm coming Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Orchestration
entries.summary: Coordinating multiple steps, tools, or models in sequence to complete a task Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Output tokens
entries.summary: The tokens the system generates in response Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Parallel processing
entries.summary: Doing thousands of calculations at the same time instead of one after another Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Persistent instructions
entries.summary: Rules you write once that load into every conversation automatically. They tell the AI who you are and how you want it to behave. Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Planning
entries.summary: Breaking a complex goal into smaller steps the agent can execute one at a time Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Pre-training
entries.summary: The big, expensive first pass where the model learns general patterns from massive data Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Prefill
entries.summary: The first phase of inference: processing your entire input at once to build an understanding of it Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Project / Workspace
entries.summary: A persistent space where instructions + files + conversations live together. Everything inside inherits the same context. Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Prompt engineering
entries.summary: The craft of phrasing instructions to get good output from a model — how you ask (2023) Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Prompt/context engineer
entries.summary: Designs the instructions, context, and workflows that make AI systems work well for specific tasks. Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Prompting
entries.summary: Phrasing your input carefully to get the output you want — the cheapest, fastest customisation Read the full explanation .

entries.title: PUE (Power Usage Effectiveness)
entries.summary: How efficiently a data centre uses electricity. 1.0 = perfect (all power goes to computing). The industry average is ~1.55 (meaning 55% of electricity goes to cooling and overhead). Best-in-class hyperscalers achieve 1.1–1.2. Read the full explanation .
aliases: what does PUE (Power Usage Effectiveness) mean

entries.title: Quantisation
entries.summary: Compressing a model's numbers (e.g. from 16-bit to 4-bit) so it runs on less hardware Read the full explanation .

entries.title: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)
entries.summary: A system that retrieves relevant documents, injects them into the context window, and lets the model generate a response grounded in that information Read the full explanation . Put it into practice .

entries.title: Recoverability
entries.summary: How well a mistake can be contained, detected and reversed before it spreads or affects someone else. Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Red-teaming
entries.summary: Deliberately attacking your own AI system (before bad actors do) to find vulnerabilities, safety failures, and edge cases Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Regression testing
entries.summary: Checking whether an update broke something that previously worked Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Research scientist
entries.summary: Invents new techniques and architectures. Publishes papers. Works at the frontier of what's possible. Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Reverse diffusion / denoising
entries.summary: The generation process of starting from noise and sculpting it into an image Read the full explanation .
aliases: what does Reverse diffusion / denoising mean

entries.title: RLHF
entries.summary: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback — humans rate outputs ("A is better than B"), and those ratings shape the model's behaviour Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Router
entries.summary: A system that decides which model handles which request — sending simple questions to cheap/fast models and complex ones to expensive/powerful ones Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Routine / Scheduled task
entries.summary: An agent task that runs automatically on a schedule (daily, weekly) without you asking each time. "Every Monday morning, synthesise my priorities for the week." Read the full explanation .
aliases: what does Routine / Scheduled task mean

entries.title: Sandbox
entries.summary: A restricted environment intended to limit what code or an automated action can reach or change. Its protections depend on the actual permissions and isolation; it reduces risk rather than guaranteeing zero consequences. Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Scaling hypothesis
entries.summary: The idea that current architectures (transformers) will reach AGI if we simply make them bigger with more data and compute Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Scaling laws
entries.summary: The finding that bigger models + more data + more compute = predictably better performance Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Semantic search
entries.summary: Searching by meaning rather than by exact keywords — "find documents about the same concept , even if they use different words" Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Sideways move
entries.summary: An iteration that's different but not clearly better. The AI changed things, but you can't say the new version is an improvement. A sign you've passed the point of useful refinement. Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Structural constraint
entries.summary: A rule that gives the AI something concrete to DO (or not do) rather than a vague prohibition. "Use only information from this document" works. "Don't make things up" doesn't. Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Supervised learning
entries.summary: Learning from labelled examples — the system gets both the question and the correct answer Read the full explanation .

entries.title: SWE-bench
entries.summary: A benchmark testing coding ability — gives the model real GitHub issues and checks if its code actually passes the tests Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Sycophancy
entries.summary: The AI's tendency to agree with everything you say, validate your framing, and avoid disagreeing even when you're wrong. A documented, measured property of how these models are trained. Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Synthetic data
entries.summary: Training data generated by AI rather than collected from the real world Read the full explanation .

entries.title: System
entries.summary: A repeatable way of working that produces consistent results without you reinventing the process each time. Not complicated automation — just a stable setup plus a few habits. Read the full explanation .

entries.title: System prompt
entries.summary: Hidden instructions loaded before your message — tells the model who it is, how to behave, what tools it has Read the full explanation . Put it into practice .

entries.title: Task fit
entries.summary: Whether the type of work you're asking for is something this particular tool does well Read the full explanation . Put it into practice .

entries.title: Temperature
entries.summary: A setting that controls randomness — low temperature = predictable/safe answers, high = creative/surprising Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Template
entries.summary: A reusable brief you've refined over multiple uses. The first time you write a brief, it's a guess. After you've used it five times and fixed what didn't work, it's a template. Read the full explanation .

entries.title: The wizard problem
entries.summary: AI speaks with the confidence of an expert whether it's right or wrong. The fluency of the output gives you no signal about whether the content is accurate. Polished and wrong look identical to polished and right. Read the full explanation .
aliases: what does The wizard problem mean

entries.title: Throughput
entries.summary: How many requests a system can handle at once — serving millions of users simultaneously Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Token
entries.summary: A chunk of text the system processes as a single unit — not a word, not a letter, something in between Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Tokenisation
entries.summary: The process of chopping input (text, images, audio) into tokens before the system can work with it Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Tool access
entries.summary: Whether the AI can do things beyond generating text: search the web, read files, run code, connect to apps. Without tools, it can only use what it already "knows" and what's in the conversation. Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Tool calling
entries.summary: When a model generates structured output that triggers a real action (search the web, send an email, run code) Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Tool-use sandbox
entries.summary: A test or simulation environment where proposed actions use fake, staged or restricted services instead of changing the real system. A draft-and-approve gate is related but is not itself always a sandbox. Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Top-k / Top-p
entries.summary: Filters that narrow down which tokens the system can pick from at each step Read the full explanation .

entries.title: TPU (Tensor Processing Unit)
entries.summary: Google's custom chip, built from scratch specifically for AI workloads — not general-purpose at all Read the full explanation .
aliases: what does TPU (Tensor Processing Unit) mean

entries.title: Training data
entries.summary: The examples a system learns from — the textbook it studies before it can do the job Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Training loop
entries.summary: The repeating cycle: guess → measure how wrong → adjust → guess again. Millions of times. Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Transformer
entries.summary: The architecture (2017) that made modern AI possible — processes all tokens in parallel and uses attention Read the full explanation .

entries.title: TSMC (Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company)
entries.summary: The company that manufactures most of the world's advanced chips — including NVIDIA's GPUs. Controls ~70% of global foundry revenue and 90%+ of leading-edge production Read the full explanation .
aliases: what is TSMC (Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company)
what does TSMC (Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company) mean

entries.title: TTS (text-to-speech)
entries.summary: Converting text into spoken audio Read the full explanation .

entries.title: TWh (Terawatt-hour)
entries.summary: A unit of energy. Global data centres used ~485 TWh in 2025 — about 1.5% of all electricity generated worldwide Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Unsupervised learning
entries.summary: Learning from unlabelled data — the system finds patterns on its own without being told the "right" answer Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Vector
entries.summary: A list of numbers. An embedding is a specific type of vector that encodes meaning. Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Vector database
entries.summary: A specialised database that stores embeddings and lets you search by similarity — "find me things similar to this" Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Vision encoder
entries.summary: A neural network that converts image patches into numbers a language model can read Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Vocabulary
entries.summary: The set of all tokens a system knows — its dictionary of chunks Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Voice profile
entries.summary: A document that captures how you write: tone, sentence patterns, vocabulary, what you never say. Built from examples of your actual writing. Read the full explanation .

entries.title: VRAM
entries.summary: The memory on a GPU chip — determines how large a model you can run Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Web crawl
entries.summary: An automated process that visits web pages, follows links, and downloads text — the way most internet training data is collected Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Weights (parameters)
entries.summary: The numbers inside the network that get adjusted during training — what the model "knows" lives in these numbers Read the full explanation .

entries.title: Wrapper
entries.summary: The user-facing layer — the interface you actually see and type into (ChatGPT's chat window, Claude's interface, a company's AI assistant) Read the full explanation .
